sources.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Arts of the Ancient Americas, Mexica
sources.note: Museum overview used only for the opening: three-member alliance, indirect patchwork empire, tribute, materials, arts, and conquest-era scope.

sources.title: Museo Nacional de Antropología: Mexica (1200 to 1521)
sources.note: National museum overview used only for the opening: Mexica naming, Tenochtitlan, alliance, Late Postclassic setting, and living archaeological record.

sources.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Mexico, 1400 to 1600 A.D.
sources.note: Chronology used for alliance formation, indirect tribute rule, Ahuitzotl expansion, autonomous Tlaxcala, Purépecha resistance, and conquest-era sequence.

sources.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Tenochtitlan
sources.note: Museum synthesis used for canals, causeways, aqueducts, markets, neighborhoods, reclaimed land, population caution, and 1521 destruction.

sources.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Tenochtitlan, Templo Mayor
sources.note: Museum essay used for twin shrines, sacred-mountain design, repeated construction phases, offerings, archaeology, and religious meaning.

sources.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Aztec Stone Sculpture
sources.note: Museum essay used for quarrying and carving technologies, tools, abrasives, transport, polychromy, and elite monument context.

sources.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Paying the Man, Ancient Tributes in Golden Kingdoms
sources.note: Museum study used for tribute commodities and the colonial date, commission, purpose, and limits of the Codex Mendoza.

sources.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Serpent labret with articulated tongue
sources.note: Object record used to distinguish Mexica Tenochtitlan, Acolhua Texcoco, and Tepaneca Tlacopan and to explain elite speech, metalwork, and office.

sources.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Drum (Teponaztli)
sources.note: Object record used for music in weddings, processions, agricultural dances, ballgames, and continued use into the colonial period.

sources.title: UNAM Noticonquista: La Triple Alianza, politics among Central Mexican Nahuas
sources.note: University history essay used for competing formation dates, member relations, political flexibility, and the danger of treating the alliance as one centralized nation-state.

sources.title: UNAM Noticonquista: Independent territories beyond the Isthmus
sources.note: University essay used for Ahuitzotl-era Oaxaca and Tehuantepec campaigns, Soconusco pressure, frontier garrisons, tribute, and patchy reach.

sources.title: UNAM Noticonquista: The military situation at the beginning of 1521
sources.note: University essay used for Indigenous coalitions, smallpox, Texcoco politics, supply lines, canoes, and the two-stage strategy against Tenochtitlan.

sources.title: INAH Lugares: Tlaxcala archaeological and historical zone
sources.note: Official Mexican heritage source used for Tlaxcalan resistance, the long Mexica blockade, and why atlas containment does not equal conquest.

sources.title: INAH Lugares: Templo Mayor
sources.note: Official archaeological-site guide used for Ahuítzotl’s 1486 to 1502 phase, causeways, subsidence, flood repairs, architecture, and restricted ritual spaces.

sources.title: INAH Lugares: Huei Tzompantli
sources.note: Official archaeological report used for the excavated skull-rack platform, construction phases, studied remains, and careful distinction from colonial numerical claims.

sources.title: INAH: Excavated chinampas and canals in a Tenochtitlan neighborhood
sources.note: Official archaeological report used for a pre-Hispanic canal-and-chinampa complex at the city’s southwest edge and preservation limits beneath modern Mexico City.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Historic Centre of Mexico City and Xochimilco
sources.note: UNESCO source used for surviving chinampa landscape, canals, constructed plots, human management of the lacustrine setting, and continuity without claiming unchanged farming.

sources.title: UNAM Noticonquista: Xochimilco, 1521
sources.note: University essay used for Xochimilco’s tributary subjection, food supply to Tenochtitlan, local interests, and later alliance choices.

sources.title: Getty Research Institute: Digital Florentine Codex
sources.note: Project history used for the 1577 manuscript, Nahua elders/authors/artists, parallel Nahuatl and Spanish columns, images, and colonial-production caveats.

sources.title: Digital Florentine Codex, Book 9, folio 1r
sources.note: Primary-source edition used for Tlatelolco merchants, trade goods, an authentic alphabetic Nahuatl sample, diplomatic transcription, and modern translation.

sources.title: Digital Florentine Codex, Book 2, folio 3r
sources.note: Primary-source edition used for eighteen twenty-day festival periods, rain and water rites, and the Christian editorial frame that shapes the account.

sources.title: Digital Florentine Codex, Book 10, folio 108r
sources.note: Primary-source edition used for named ingredients and treatments while warning that recorded remedies are historical evidence, not medical advice or proof of efficacy.

sources.title: Digital Florentine Codex, Book 6, folio 129v
sources.note: Primary-source edition used for midwives, pregnancy care, steam-bath context, speech, and colonial compilation limits.

sources.title: Digital Florentine Codex, Book 8, folio 28v
sources.note: Primary-source edition used for palace stores, maize, beans, chia, amaranth, salt, chile, squash seeds, stewards, and tribute gatherers.

sources.title: University of Kentucky: Codex Mendoza, folio 60 recto
sources.note: University digital exhibit used for colonial pictorial scenes of children’s chores, gendered training, age dots, household economy, and retrospective-source limits.

sources.title: Yale eHRAF World Cultures: Aztec culture summary
sources.note: University synthesis used for social ranks, gendered labor, common foods and drinks, household craft learning, schools, and variation by status.

sources.title: INAH repository: Mexico, From the Olmecs to the Aztecs
sources.note: National anthropology repository edition used for food, clothing, household teaching, schooling, status, and the limits of colonial daily-life reconstruction.

sources.title: Tufts University Tisch Library: The Badianus Manuscript
sources.note: University special-collections guide used for the 1552 Nahua herbal, Martín de la Cruz, Juan Badiano, medicinal plants, Latin translation, and colonial institutional context.

sources.title: UNAM record: Potable water and sanitation in Tenochtitlan, Aztec culture
sources.note: University research record used for potable-water works, lack of a citywide sewer, reported privies, canoe collection of excrement, and evidentiary caution.

sources.title: United Nations University: The Aztecs of Mexico, a zero-waste society
sources.note: UN University synthesis used for organic-waste reuse, chinampa fertilizer, canal transport, and the limits and health risks of romanticizing waste recycling.

sources.title: INAH: Tlaloc and Chapultepec, a place consecrated to water
sources.note: Official heritage source used for Chapultepec springs, connected cisterns and channels, hydraulic engineering, rulers, and sacred associations.

sources.title: INAH: Urbanism and architecture at Tlatelolco
sources.note: Official archaeological publication used for unequal fresh-water distribution, elite conduits, water carriers, and the Acuecuexco aqueduct flood tradition.

sources.title: Library of Congress: Huexotzinco Codex, 1531
sources.note: National library record used for Indigenous pictorial testimony, taxation lawsuit, eight amatl panels, 1531 date, and respect/context note.

sources.title: Smarthistory: The Codex Huexotzinco
sources.note: Scholarly art-history essay used for Indigenous agency, tribute-document traditions, Huexotzinco’s opposition to Mexica expansion, and colonial entanglement.

sources.title: INPI National Catalogue: Nahua / Náhuatl people
sources.note: Official Indigenous-peoples catalogue used for living Nahua communities, wide regional distribution, language variation, and contemporary cultural diversity.

sources.title: INAH educational poster: Schools in Mexica culture
sources.note: Official educational material used cautiously for calmecac, telpochcalli, ichpochcalli, discipline, learning, and gender/status distinctions.

sources.title: UNAM Noticonquista: War in Tlatelolco in 1521
sources.note: University reconstruction used for the final siege, Indigenous coalition forces, lake warfare, capture of the market, and the end of organized imperial resistance.

proposedOverrides.summary: The atlas’s 1492 to 1500 display slice of the Triple Alliance, a polity that historically existed from about 1428 to 1521.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact indexed target is present once at 1492 and missing a card and override.
The separate aztec-empire id represents the same Triple Alliance historically and replaces the target at the 1500 map seam.
The 1492 polygon is an imported display footprint, not a surveyed border or an ethnicity map.
The ring incorrectly contains unconquered Tlaxcala and overlaps multiple contemporary cultural/language features.
Mexihcah most directly names the Mexica of Tenochtitlan; Texcoco and Tlacopan were distinct partners.
The override preserves the indexed 1492 to 1500 interval and records no fall because 1500 is an identifier swap.
